relevant_findings.topic: Aluminum siding has two valid repaint substrate states
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike vinyl siding repaint (single state SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT), aluminum siding repaint has TWO valid substrate states: SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT (existing coating adhered, minimal chalk) and SS_EXT_CHALKING (existing coating chalky but adhered, chalk transfers on touch). Both states are repaintable but SS_EXT_CHALKING requires significantly more prep labor for chalk removal. Aluminum does not progress to SS_EXT_FAILING_PAINT or SS_EXT_PEELING under normal conditions — the factory-baked enamel bonds metallurgically to the aluminum substrate rather than mechanically like wood paint.

relevant_findings.topic: Al2O3 oxide layer is the primary adhesion barrier
relevant_findings.finding: Aluminum forms a stable aluminum oxide (Al2O3) film on exposure to air. This oxide layer is chemically inert and prevents standard coatings from achieving mechanical or chemical adhesion. Successful coating of aluminum requires deoxidation and etching of the surface — standard exterior primers and even adhesion primers (STIX class) designed for vinyl/PVC do NOT work on aluminum. Self-etching primers containing phosphoric acid are the ONLY primer class that addresses this chemistry.

relevant_findings.topic: Self-etching primer is mandatory with strict DFT limits
relevant_findings.finding: Self-etching primers (phosphoric acid + zinc chromate formulation) are required for all aluminum siding repaint. The acid component etches through the Al2O3 oxide layer while zinc provides galvanic corrosion resistance. DFT MUST be held to 0.5-1.0 mils — this is a critical application parameter. Excessive primer thickness (>1.0 mil) causes cohesive failure WITHIN the primer film itself, not at the primer-substrate interface. This is a unique failure mode specific to self-etching chemistry — the acid-etch reaction zone has limited depth, and primer beyond that zone has no bond substrate.

relevant_findings.topic: Complete chalk removal is a mandatory gate before primer
relevant_findings.finding: Aluminum siding chalking is more severe than vinyl chalking. Chalking on aluminum occurs as the factory-baked enamel degrades from UV exposure, releasing pigment particles as powder. Any residual chalk powder acts as a bond-breaker between the self-etching primer and the aluminum substrate — the acid cannot reach the metal surface through chalk residue. Chalk removal is a mandatory gate: chalk verification test (hand-rub with dark cloth) must pass BEFORE primer application. This is not a quality preference — it is a structural bond requirement.

relevant_findings.topic: Chalk severity drives prep labor, not primer selection
relevant_findings.finding: chalk_severity (none/light/heavy) is a configuration dimension that drives PREP LABOR TIME, not primer chemistry. All chalk severity paths converge at the same requirement: complete chalk removal before priming. However, heavy chalk requires significantly more wash time (multiple passes, TSP concentration, dwell time), possible mechanical scrubbing, and extended dry time. None = standard wash, light = TSP wash with verification, heavy = multiple wash passes + mechanical scrub + extended verification protocol.

relevant_findings.topic: 180-320 grit scuff required to break oxide layer
relevant_findings.finding: After washing and chalk removal, aluminum surfaces must be scuffed with synthetic steel wool or 180-320 grit abrasive pads to mechanically break the Al2O3 oxide film. This is a more aggressive prep step than vinyl's light scuff (which is for adhesion tooth only). The oxide-breaking scuff exposes fresh aluminum metal for the self-etching primer's acid component to react with. Timing between scuff and primer application matters — aluminum re-oxidizes rapidly in ambient air.

relevant_findings.topic: Coastal environment triggers epoxy primer intermediate layer
relevant_findings.finding: In marine or harsh coastal environments (salt air exposure), an epoxy primer intermediate layer is added between the self-etching primer and the finish topcoat. This creates a three-layer system: self-etch primer (0.5-1.0 mil) -> epoxy intermediate (per manufacturer spec) -> acrylic topcoat. The epoxy layer provides additional corrosion resistance and chemical barrier that standard acrylic topcoats cannot provide alone in salt-laden environments. This is a conditional modifier triggered by site environment, not a standard part of every aluminum repaint.

relevant_findings.topic: No LRV restriction — aluminum conducts heat without warping
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike vinyl siding (LRV <35 hard stop, LRV 35-55 requires IR-reflective products), aluminum siding has NO LRV restriction. Aluminum is a metal that conducts heat efficiently — it does not trap heat at the surface like PVC. Aluminum's melting point (1220 degrees F) is vastly above any surface temperature achievable from solar gain. Dark colors are fully permissible on aluminum siding without thermal distortion risk. This eliminates the lrv_class configuration dimension entirely.

relevant_findings.topic: Spray is primary application method — no backbrushing needed
relevant_findings.finding: Airless spray is the primary application method for aluminum siding field, same as vinyl. Aluminum is non-porous — coating does not absorb into the substrate, so backbrushing serves no purpose. Brush/roller detail work is needed only for J-channels, under-sill channels, and cut-in at trim transitions. Production rates: spray 400-500 SF/hr, brush detail 125-175 SF/hr.

relevant_findings.topic: No RRP/lead gate — aluminum siding is post-1960s product
relevant_findings.finding: Aluminum siding is a post-1960s residential product. The factory-baked enamel coating was never lead-based. EPA Lead-Safe RRP requirements do not apply to aluminum siding repaint. This eliminates a major cost variable present in wood siding repaint specs. Note: aluminum siding predates vinyl siding in the market (aluminum popular 1940s-1970s, vinyl replaced it 1960s+), but even the earliest residential aluminum siding used baked enamel, not lead paint.
relevant_findings.source: Researcher analysis; aluminum siding product history

relevant_findings.topic: Oxide reformation timing is critical — prime promptly after prep
relevant_findings.finding: Aluminum re-oxidizes rapidly when exposed to air after the oxide layer is mechanically broken. The self-etching primer should be applied within a reasonable time window after scuffing to ensure the acid component reacts with fresh aluminum rather than reformed oxide. Doctrine does not specify an exact time window. Industry practice suggests 4-8 hours in normal conditions, shorter in humid or salt-air environments. This is primarily an SOP scheduling concern, not an estimation variable.

When multiple coats are applied, labor distributes: 1st coat = 50% of total labor (full prep, first pass, learning the surface), 2nd coat = 30% (familiar surface, better coverage), 3rd coat = 20% (smooth surface, minimal touch-up). Standard aluminum repaint system: self-etching primer + 1-2 finish coats depending on quality tier. Coastal variant adds epoxy intermediate coat.

relevant_findings.topic: Pressure washing is mandatory first step with chalk-specific protocol
relevant_findings.finding: All aluminum siding repaint requires pressure washing as the first production step. For aluminum, the wash protocol is more rigorous than vinyl: alkaline cleaner (TSP or dedicated siding cleaner), downward spray pattern, and chalk-specific verification after drying. Wash rate: 500-1000 SF/hr baseline, but heavily chalked aluminum drops to the lower end (or below) due to multiple passes and dwell time. Must dry completely before scuffing and priming.

relevant_findings.topic: PCA P14 Level 2 is the baseline prep standard for aluminum siding
relevant_findings.finding: PCA P14 governs surface preparation levels for exterior siding. Level 2 (Standard) is the baseline for exterior siding repaints. For aluminum, this includes washing with chalk removal verification, mechanical scuffing of the oxide layer (180-320 grit), and self-etching primer application. More intensive than vinyl Level 2 (which is wash + light scuff only) because of the oxide layer treatment requirement.

condition_drivers.impact: Two valid states. SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT: standard prep (wash, scuff, prime). SS_EXT_CHALKING: extended prep (intensive wash + chalk verification gate + scuff + prime). Both states require self-etching primer — primer chemistry does not change by state. State drives PREP LABOR TIME, not material path. SS_EXT_CHALKING adds 1.40x prep modifier per Substrate_State_Reference.md.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a CONFIGURATION DIMENSION with two valid values. More complex than vinyl (one state) but simpler than wood siding repaint (five states). Aluminum in failing/peeling condition is typically re-clad, not repainted.

condition_drivers.impact: QT2: economy — wash, self-etching prime, single finish coat spray. QT3: standard — wash with TSP + chalk verification, self-etching prime, two finish coats, brush detail at J-channels and cut-in. Caulk assessment at siding-to-trim joints. QT3 adds the detail coat for J-channels, under-sill areas, and cut-in quality — same labor differentiation as vinyl.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a CONFIGURATION DIMENSION. No QT4/QT5 — aluminum siding is not a fine-finish substrate. Same tier range as vinyl repaint.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep labor pathway. none = standard wash (baseline). light = TSP wash + chalk verification test + possible re-wash. heavy = multiple wash passes + mechanical scrubbing + extended dwell time + mandatory re-verification. All paths converge at complete chalk removal before priming. chalk_severity does NOT change primer chemistry or material selection — it changes wash and prep labor time only.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a CONFIGURATION DIMENSION unique to aluminum siding repaint. Replaces lrv_class from vinyl (aluminum has no LRV restriction). See RC-001 for rationale on keeping this as a dimension despite all paths requiring complete removal.

condition_drivers.impact: Spray is primary method for aluminum siding field. No backbrushing required (non-porous metal substrate). Brush/roll for J-channels and detail only, or when spray is not feasible (wind, neighbor proximity). Method affects protection zone escalation (spray = more masking of adjacent surfaces).
condition_drivers.notes: This is a CONFIGURATION DIMENSION. Note: NO spray_backbrush option — aluminum does not absorb coating, so backbrushing serves no purpose. Identical to vinyl in this regard.

condition_drivers.impact: Height modifier on all tasks at elevation. ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. Applied per elevation. Simpler than wood siding repaint — no DSD stacking. Same access modifier structure as vinyl repaint.
condition_drivers.notes: Treated as a HEIGHT MODIFIER (like FAC_HEIGHT for interior), not a site condition. Simpler cost impact than wood repaint because no DSD dimension.

quality_differences.description: Economy aluminum siding repaint. Pressure wash with detergent (chalk removal verification if chalking present). Scuff oxide layer 180-320 grit. Self-etching primer spray, single coat at 0.5-1.0 mil DFT. Single finish coat, 100% acrylic exterior spray. Minimal J-channel detail. No caulk replacement.
quality_differences.typical_use: Rental property, budget-constrained, pre-sale cosmetic refresh, color change on sound aluminum siding.

quality_differences.description: Standard residential aluminum siding repaint. Pressure wash with TSP or alkaline cleaner, full chalk removal verification (hand-rub test with dark cloth). Scuff oxide layer 180-320 grit. Self-etching primer spray at 0.5-1.0 mil DFT. Two finish coats with mid-grade 100% acrylic exterior. Brush detail at J-channels, under-sill channels, and trim transitions. Caulk assessment at siding-to-trim joints.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard homeowner repaint, color change, fade restoration on aluminum siding. Most common tier.

failure_modes.name: Chalk-induced peeling — residual chalk not fully removed
failure_modes.description: Residual chalk powder remaining on aluminum surface after washing acts as a bond-breaker. Self-etching primer bonds to chalk layer instead of aluminum substrate. Entire coating system peels at the chalk interface — primer, topcoat, and all. Peeling appears within 12-24 months, typically beginning on south and west exposures where original chalking was most severe.
failure_modes.prevention: Mandatory chalk verification gate after wash and dry. Hand-rub test with dark cloth — any white transfer = re-wash required. Multiple wash passes for heavy chalk. Do not prime until chalk verification passes. Document verification in QC log.
failure_modes.detection: Patchy peeling concentrated on sun-exposed facades. White chalk powder visible on back of peeled coating. Peeling at primer-substrate interface (not cohesive). Onset 12-24 months.

failure_modes.name: Cohesive primer failure — self-etching primer applied too thick
failure_modes.description: Self-etching primer applied above 1.0 mil DFT fails cohesively WITHIN the primer film. The acid-etch reaction creates a bond zone of limited depth at the primer-metal interface. Primer material beyond that reaction zone has no bond substrate — it is essentially unbonded primer sitting on top of bonded primer. Under thermal cycling or mechanical stress, the primer film splits at the bond-zone boundary. This is NOT an adhesion failure at the metal surface — it is a COHESIVE failure within the primer itself.
failure_modes.prevention: Strict DFT control: 0.5-1.0 mil ONLY. Use wet film thickness gauge during application. Airless spray tip selection must match thin-film requirement (fine-atomization tips). One pass coverage — do not double-back. Train applicators on this specific failure mode. QC spot-check DFT with dry film gauge after cure.
failure_modes.detection: Primer layer splits — bottom layer adhered to metal, top layer peeling with topcoat. Visible primer film delamination (not clean peel from metal). Can occur within months, not years.

failure_modes.name: Oxide reformation — primer applied too late after surface prep
failure_modes.description: Aluminum re-oxidizes rapidly when the Al2O3 layer is mechanically broken by scuffing. If self-etching primer is not applied within a reasonable window (4-8 hours typical), the oxide reforms and the acid component must re-etch through new oxide. Extended delays (24+ hours) may result in oxide thick enough to reduce primer bond quality, especially in humid or coastal environments where oxidation is accelerated.
failure_modes.prevention: Schedule scuffing and priming as sequential tasks on the same work day. In coastal environments, reduce the window to 2-4 hours. If delay is unavoidable, re-scuff before priming. SOP should enforce same-day scuff-to-prime sequencing.
failure_modes.detection: Premature adhesion failure in patches corresponding to areas where delay between scuff and prime was longest. Adhesion pull test shows lower values than expected.

failure_modes.name: Standard primer substitution — non-self-etching primer used on aluminum
failure_modes.description: Standard exterior primers, bonding primers (STIX class for vinyl), and general-purpose adhesion primers do NOT bond to aluminum's Al2O3 oxide layer. They sit on the surface without chemical reaction. Entire coating system peels from aluminum in sheets, often within the first thermal cycle season. This is a material specification error, not an application error.
failure_modes.prevention: Lock primer specification to self-etching primer containing phosphoric acid and zinc. QC verification at material delivery — check product label and PDS for self-etching designation. Do NOT accept substitutions. STIX-class adhesion primers are NOT equivalent — they are designed for PVC/vinyl, not aluminum oxide.
failure_modes.detection: Complete coating system peeling in large sheets from aluminum surface. Clean separation — aluminum surface intact with no primer residue. Onset within first 6-12 months.

failure_modes.name: Corrosion breakthrough in coastal environment without epoxy intermediate
failure_modes.description: In marine or harsh coastal environments, salt-laden air penetrates through standard acrylic topcoat to the primer layer. Without the epoxy intermediate barrier, salt reaches the aluminum substrate through micro-porosity in the self-etching primer, initiating galvanic corrosion at the coating-metal interface. Corrosion undermines coating adhesion from beneath, causing blistering and eventual peeling.
failure_modes.prevention: Coastal environment trigger: when site is within salt-air exposure zone, add epoxy primer intermediate layer between self-etching primer and acrylic topcoat. Three-layer system: self-etch -> epoxy -> acrylic. Verify coastal classification during site assessment.
failure_modes.detection: Blistering of coating system, concentrated on windward facades facing ocean/bay. Corrosion staining (white aluminum oxide powder) visible at blister edges. Onset 2-5 years in coastal without epoxy intermediate.

failure_modes.name: Painting over dented or damaged aluminum panels
failure_modes.description: Dented or physically damaged aluminum panels trap moisture in deformations. Painting over dents does not address the structural damage and creates differential expansion stress at dent edges. Paint cracking at dent perimeters and moisture-induced corrosion beneath the coating at dent sites.
failure_modes.prevention: Assess aluminum panel condition during scope. Dented panels should be straightened or replaced before painting. Document panel condition in scope capture. Severely damaged panels are replacement scope, not painting scope.
failure_modes.detection: Paint cracking following the outline of existing dents. White corrosion powder at dent edges under coating.

research_corrections.corrected_to: Keep chalk_severity as configuration dimension because it drives PREP LABOR TIME, not primer selection. All paths lead to full chalk removal, but: none = standard wash (no chalk to remove, but still verified), light = TSP wash + verification + possible re-wash, heavy = multiple wash passes + mechanical scrubbing + extended dwell time + mandatory re-verification. The labor difference between none and heavy is significant (potentially 2-3x prep time on wash step alone). Dimension is justified by labor impact.

Doctrine +50% is a simplified approximation — use the canonical access_type modifiers from Site_Condition_Vocabulary_Reference for estimation: ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. The doctrine +50% represents the ladder tier (1.35-1.50 range). No correction needed — confirm alignment and use canonical values.

Recommendation: SOP should enforce same-day scuff-to-prime sequencing.

key_decisions.decision: This spec covers ONLY aluminum siding. Vinyl siding is excluded — it has a separate spec (SF_SIDING_VINYL_EXT_RP_v1).
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum and vinyl have fundamentally different prep protocols (aluminum = self-etching primer + oxide deoxidation; vinyl = STIX adhesion primer + solvent attack on PVC), different failure modes (aluminum = cohesive primer failure from over-thickness; vinyl = thermal warping from dark colors), different material constraints (aluminum = no LRV restriction; vinyl = LRV hard stop), and different substrate states (aluminum = 2 states; vinyl = 1 state). Combining them would create excessive branching.

key_decisions.topic: Two substrate states — SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT and SS_EXT_CHALKING
key_decisions.decision: Two valid input states: SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT (existing coating in good condition) and SS_EXT_CHALKING (existing coating chalky but adhered).
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum's factory-baked enamel degrades through chalking as a primary failure pathway. Sound paint requires standard prep. Chalking requires intensive chalk removal prep — a significant labor difference. Both states are repaintable. Aluminum does not commonly progress to failing/peeling/weathered states like wood — severely deteriorated aluminum siding is typically re-clad rather than repainted.

key_decisions.decision: chalk_severity is a configuration dimension with values: none, light, heavy. Drives prep labor pathway.
key_decisions.rationale: Although all chalk severity paths converge at the same requirement (complete removal), the labor to achieve removal varies dramatically: none = baseline wash, light = TSP + verification, heavy = multiple passes + mechanical scrub + extended verification. This is the dominant cost variable for aluminum siding prep. Replaces lrv_class from vinyl (aluminum has no LRV concern) and partially replaces DSD from wood (aluminum has simpler deterioration).

key_decisions.topic: QT2-QT3 only — aluminum siding is not a fine-finish substrate
key_decisions.decision: Quality tier range limited to QT2 and QT3.
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum siding is a utilitarian exterior cladding with uniform factory texture. No wood grain, no architectural detail, no handcrafted character. QT4/QT5 prep and inspection standards provide no meaningful quality improvement on aluminum. The difference between QT2 and QT3 is coat count, J-channel detail, and caulk assessment — same as vinyl.

key_decisions.topic: Self-etching primer mandatory — phosphoric acid + zinc, 0.5-1.0 mil DFT max
key_decisions.decision: Self-etching primer is ALWAYS required. DFT must be held to 0.5-1.0 mil maximum. No exceptions.
key_decisions.rationale: Self-etching chemistry (phosphoric acid etches Al2O3 oxide, zinc provides galvanic corrosion resistance) is the ONLY primer system that bonds to aluminum. STIX-class adhesion primers (used for vinyl) do NOT work on aluminum oxide. The 0.5-1.0 mil DFT limit is structural — exceeding it causes cohesive failure within the primer film. This is unlike any other primer in the pipeline where more primer = better bond.

key_decisions.topic: DFT-critical primer application — over-application = cohesive failure
key_decisions.decision: Self-etching primer DFT is a CRITICAL application parameter. Over-application causes cohesive failure (unique risk).
key_decisions.rationale: The acid-etch reaction creates a bond zone of limited depth. Primer beyond that zone has no bond substrate. Over-application creates an internal weak plane in the primer film. This requires: fine-atomization spray tips, single-pass technique, wet film gauge checks during application, dry film gauge QC after cure. SOP must specifically train for this failure mode.

key_decisions.topic: Coastal environment modifier — triggers epoxy primer intermediate layer
key_decisions.decision: Coastal/marine environments trigger addition of an epoxy primer intermediate layer between self-etching primer and acrylic topcoat.
key_decisions.rationale: Salt air penetrates standard acrylic topcoat to reach the primer-metal interface, initiating galvanic corrosion. Epoxy intermediate provides a chemical-resistant barrier. Creates a three-layer system: self-etch -> epoxy -> acrylic. This is a conditional modifier, not standard — applies only when site assessment indicates salt-air exposure.

key_decisions.topic: No LRV restriction — aluminum conducts heat, no thermal warping risk
key_decisions.decision: No LRV class restriction, no LRV hard stop, no IR-reflective product requirement. Any color is permitted.
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum is a metal conductor — heat dissipates through the panel rather than concentrating at the surface. Aluminum's melting point (1220 degrees F) is vastly above solar-gain temperatures. This eliminates the lrv_class dimension entirely (major simplification vs vinyl). Dark colors are fully permissible.

key_decisions.topic: No RRP/lead gate — aluminum siding is post-1960s product
key_decisions.decision: EPA Lead-Safe RRP is NOT applicable to aluminum siding repaint.
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum siding's factory-baked enamel finish was never lead-based. Even the earliest residential aluminum siding (1940s-1950s) used baked enamel, not lead paint. RRP requirements do not apply. This eliminates a major cost variable present in wood siding repaint specs.

key_decisions.topic: Spray primary application — brush detail for J-channels and cut-in only
key_decisions.decision: Airless spray is primary method. NO backbrushing required. Brush detail only for J-channels and cut-in.
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum is non-porous metal — coating does not absorb into the substrate. Backbrushing serves no purpose on metal. Production rate for spray (400-500 SF/hr) is higher than wood siding (which requires backbrush). Same spray strategy as vinyl repaint.

key_decisions.topic: Complete chalk removal = mandatory gate — chalk verification test before prime
key_decisions.decision: Chalk verification test is a mandatory gate. Work CANNOT proceed to priming until chalk verification passes.
key_decisions.rationale: Residual chalk is a structural bond-breaker for self-etching primer. The acid component must contact metal or sound coating — chalk powder prevents this contact. Hand-rub test with dark cloth is the verification method. Any white transfer = re-wash required. This is documented as a gate in the SOP, not a quality preference.

key_decisions.topic: Oxide reformation concern — primer timing after surface prep is critical
key_decisions.decision: Scuffing and priming should be scheduled as sequential same-day tasks. 4-8 hour window typical, 2-4 hours coastal.
key_decisions.rationale: Aluminum re-oxidizes rapidly in ambient air. The mechanical scuff exposes fresh metal for acid-etch reaction. Extended delays allow oxide reformation, reducing primer bond quality. This is an SOP scheduling constraint. If delay is unavoidable, re-scuff before priming.

notes_for_materials_manager: Primer: ALWAYS self-etching primer (phosphoric acid + zinc chromate formulation). Examples: Rust-Oleum Self-Etching Primer, Sherwin-Williams Wash Primer, PPG DP Series. These are the ONLY primers that chemically bond to aluminum oxide. STIX-class adhesion primers are NOT acceptable — they are designed for PVC, not aluminum oxide.

CRITICAL DFT limit: Self-etching primer must be applied at 0.5-1.0 mil DFT ONLY. Over-application causes cohesive failure. Source products with coverage rate guidance that achieves this DFT range. Fine-atomization spray tips required.

Finish coat: 100% acrylic latex exterior recommended for durability and flexibility. No binder restriction as strict as vinyl (no thermal warping concern), but acrylic is the standard. Alkyd finish over self-etch primer is acceptable but uncommon in residential.
NO LRV restriction — any color is permitted on aluminum siding. No need to source IR-reflective products. This is simpler than vinyl material sourcing.

Coastal environment: Source epoxy primer for intermediate coat when coastal modifier is triggered. Epoxy must be compatible with self-etching primer below and acrylic topcoat above. Verify inter-coat compatibility on PDS.

Coverage rates on aluminum: self-etching primer 400-500 SF/gal (thin film, 0.5-1.0 mil). Finish coat 350-450 SF/gal (smooth metal surface). Better coverage than wood siding due to non-porous metal substrate.
Chalk removal cleaning products: TSP (trisodium phosphate) or dedicated aluminum siding cleaner. Source in bulk for heavy chalk severity projects.
Abrasive supplies: 180-320 grit abrasive pads or synthetic steel wool for oxide layer scuffing. More aggressive than vinyl prep (which uses light scuff only).
Caulk for siding-to-trim joints (QT3 only): siliconized acrylic paintable caulk. Aluminum has minimal thermal movement at joints compared to vinyl — polyurethane not required.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Module structure: setup -> protect -> wash -> chalk_verify -> scuff -> prime -> apply -> detail -> cleanup -> teardown. NOTE: chalk_verify is a GATE module — work cannot proceed to scuff/prime until chalk verification passes.

Wash module is MANDATORY first production step. Pressure wash with alkaline cleaner (TSP or siding cleaner) in downward spray pattern. Chalk removal protocol varies by chalk_severity: none = standard wash; light = TSP wash + verification; heavy = multiple passes + mechanical scrubbing + extended dwell time.

Chalk verification gate: After wash and dry, hand-rub test with dark cloth on multiple locations (prioritize south/west facades). Any white chalk transfer = re-wash required. Document verification pass in QC log. This gate applies to ALL chalk_severity levels including 'none' (verification confirms no hidden chalk).

Scuff module: 180-320 grit abrasive pads or synthetic steel wool over entire surface. Purpose: break Al2O3 oxide layer to expose fresh aluminum for acid-etch primer reaction. More aggressive than vinyl scuff. TIMING CRITICAL: prime within 4-8 hours of scuff (2-4 hours coastal) to prevent oxide reformation.

Prime module: self-etching primer spray application, single coat. DFT 0.5-1.0 mil MAXIMUM. Fine-atomization spray tip required. Single-pass technique — do not double-back. Wet film thickness gauge checks during application. DFT IS CRITICAL — over-application causes cohesive failure. Train applicators specifically on this failure mode.
Coastal variant: Add epoxy intermediate coat module between prime and apply. Follow epoxy manufacturer's inter-coat timing and DFT specifications.
Apply module: spray application, 100% acrylic latex exterior. QT2 = single finish coat. QT3 = two finish coats. NO backbrushing — aluminum is non-porous.
Detail module (QT3 only): brush detail at J-channels, under-sill channels, corner transitions, and trim cut-in. Rate: 125-175 SF/hr.
No RRP module — aluminum siding factory enamel is not lead-based.
No LRV verification gate — aluminum has no LRV restriction (unlike vinyl SOP which requires LRV gate).
No warranty void acknowledgment — aluminum siding manufacturer warranties have typically expired on repaint-age siding. Unlike vinyl where warranty void is a current concern.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: This spec is SIMILAR in complexity to vinyl siding repaint but with different cost drivers. Primary variables: SF quantity x chalk_severity prep modifier x access modifier x coat count.

Production rates (QT3 baseline, ground access): pressure wash 500-1000 SF/hr (lower for heavy chalk), masking/prep 150-250 SF/hr, oxide scuff 200-300 SF/hr (new task vs vinyl), self-etching prime spray 350-450 SF/hr, finish coat spray 400-500 SF/hr, brush/roller detail 125-175 SF/hr.

chalk_severity labor impact on wash task: none = baseline (use upper range 800-1000 SF/hr), light = moderate (use mid-range 500-700 SF/hr), heavy = intensive (use lower range 300-500 SF/hr, may require multiple passes counted as separate tasks).
Scuff task is NEW vs vinyl repaint. Oxide layer scuffing at 200-300 SF/hr is a distinct task that vinyl does not have (vinyl has minimal scuff included in prep). This adds meaningful labor.
Access modifier is the primary multiplicative labor modifier: ground=1.00, ladder=1.35, scaffold=1.60, lift=1.50. No DSD stacking (same as vinyl). No LRV stacking.
Coat system standard: self-etching prime (1 coat always) + finish coats (QT2=1, QT3=2). Total coats: QT2=2 (prime+1), QT3=3 (prime+2).
Coat system coastal: self-etching prime (1 coat) + epoxy intermediate (1 coat) + finish coats. Total coats: QT2=3, QT3=4. Coastal adds one coat to all tiers.
Multi-coat time distribution (50-30-20): apply to spray coating tasks.
Substrate state modifier: SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT prep modifier = 1.10. SS_EXT_CHALKING prep modifier = 1.40. Per Substrate_State_Reference.md. This stacks with chalk_severity on wash tasks specifically.
No LRV impact on labor or materials — any color permitted. Simpler than vinyl estimation (no lrv_class branching).
Fixed-time tasks (per project, not area-scaled): chalk verification gate (low labor — visual inspection + hand-rub test), equipment setup/teardown.
J-channel detail labor: estimate at 5-10% of total field SF as detail SF, applied at brush detail rate (125-175 SF/hr). Only at QT3. Same as vinyl.
No caulk replacement at QT2. QT3 includes caulk assessment — estimate 50-100 LF of caulk at siding-to-trim joints per typical residential project.
Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, sun, temp) are EXCLUDED from estimation — SOP/process concerns only. Per established exterior spec convention.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: Landscape protection from wash runoff and spray overspray. Brush/roll: drop cloth at base. Spray: full tarp over plantings + spray shield.
Mask windows during spray operations. Paper or masking film over glass. Only needed for spray method.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: Mask trim elements when trim is different color from siding. Tape line at junction for brush/roll. Full paper mask for spray.
Mask exterior doors during spray operations. Full cover with masking film or plastic.
Cover AC units, heat pumps, and utility panels within spray zone. Full tarp coverage.
Protect soffit/fascia at eave junction if not being painted in same project. Tape line or paper border at siding-to-soffit transition.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray
zones.notes: Patios, walkways, and driveways within work zone. Drop cloth for brush/roll. Full tarp for spray.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Window and door protection during siding work is NOT this spec's responsibility when those surfaces have their own spec. If windows/doors are not being painted, their protection is scoped under this spec's masking zones. Protection responsibility follows surface ownership.
protection_zones_analysis.repaint_specific_note: Repaint on occupied homes has additional protection considerations: vehicles in driveways, outdoor furniture, pet areas. Client communication about work zone access is SOP, not estimation. Aluminum siding wash generates more runoff than vinyl wash due to chalk removal chemistry — landscape protection is especially important.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Corner trim at building corners. Often different (trim) color. Siding terminates at corner trim. Separate spec.
Window casing trim around openings. Siding terminates at casing. Separate spec.
Door casing trim. Same as window casing relationship. Separate spec.
Fascia at roofline. Often white/light trim color. Separate spec.
Soffit underside at eave. Siding terminates at soffit/frieze junction. Separate spec.
Foundation below siding starter strip. Not painted in this scope.
Frieze board between siding and soffit. Trim color. Separate spec.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Siding field has NO edge work requirements. All adjacent surfaces are separate specs. Protection relationships only. Siding terminates at trim boards — no wet-edge blending across specs. Identical adjacency pattern as vinyl siding repaint and wood siding repaint.

affected_conditions.notes: Access type drives a HEIGHT MODIFIER on tasks. Applied per elevation. Same modifier structure as vinyl repaint — no DSD stacking.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions are NOT estimatable. They are unpredictable at bid time and belong in SOP/process documentation, not production rate modifiers. Per established exterior spec convention.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Critical for spray but not estimatable.
Varies by time of day, sun angle, season. Not predictable at bid time. SOP concern.
Weather-dependent. Self-etching primer requires dry substrate but dew point is not predictable at bid time.
Varies by elevation and season. Important for oxide reformation rate but not estimatable at bid time.

valid_input_states.rationale: Aluminum siding has TWO valid input states. SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT: existing factory-baked enamel is intact and adhered with minimal or no chalk. SS_EXT_CHALKING: existing enamel is chalky but still adhered to aluminum substrate — chalk transfers on touch. Both states are repaintable with appropriate prep. Aluminum does not commonly progress to SS_EXT_FAILING_PAINT or SS_EXT_PEELING — the factory-baked enamel bond is metallurgical. Severely deteriorated aluminum = re-cladding scope.

output_state.rationale: Output state is the new painted finish over aluminum. Satin or flat are common exterior sheens. Actual output varies by sheen selection.

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Adjacent trim may be freshly painted (protect from siding spray overspray) or awaiting its own repaint (light mask sufficient).
Soffit at eave junction. If already repainted, light mask. If awaiting repaint, no protection needed.
Foundation wall is typically unpainted. Ground-level drop cloth handled by landscape/hardscape protection zones.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Aluminum siding with existing factory-baked enamel or previously applied paint in good condition. Coating is adhered, no peeling, minimal or no chalk. Surface may have light dirt or mildew — addressed by washing.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Pressure wash with alkaline cleaner (500-1000 PSI, downward pattern). Dry 24-48 hours. Chalk verification test (hand-rub with dark cloth) — should pass easily. Scuff with 180-320 grit abrasive pads to break Al2O3 oxide layer. Prime within 4-8 hours of scuff.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Self-etching primer (phosphoric acid + zinc) — always required, no exceptions. DFT 0.5-1.0 mil ONLY.
exterior_substrate_states.dsd_range: Not applicable — aluminum has no DSD gradient
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Baseline state for aluminum siding repaint. Factory-baked enamel provides sound substrate for self-etching primer reaction. Less prep-intensive than SS_EXT_CHALKING. Prep modifier: 1.10x per Substrate_State_Reference.md.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Aluminum siding with existing coating that has developed significant chalk from UV degradation. Chalk powder transfers readily on touch. Coating beneath the chalk layer is still adhered to aluminum substrate — not peeling or failing. Chalk severity varies from light to heavy.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Intensive pressure wash with TSP or alkaline siding cleaner. Multiple passes may be required for heavy chalk. Mechanical scrubbing of stubborn areas. Extended dwell time between wash passes. Mandatory chalk verification gate after drying — hand-rub test with dark cloth. Re-wash if chalk persists. Scuff with 180-320 grit after chalk verification passes. Prime within 4-8 hours of scuff.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Self-etching primer (phosphoric acid + zinc) — same as SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT. Chalk severity does NOT change primer chemistry.
exterior_substrate_states.dsd_range: Not applicable — chalk_severity dimension addresses this spectrum
exterior_substrate_states.pca_level: PCA P14 Level 2 (Standard) with extended chalk removal protocol
exterior_substrate_states.notes: More prep-intensive state. Chalk removal is the dominant labor driver. All chalk must be completely removed before priming — residual chalk is a structural bond-breaker. Prep modifier: 1.40x per Substrate_State_Reference.md. chalk_severity (none/light/heavy) further modulates wash labor within this state.

exterior_access_type_analysis.treatment: Modifier on tasks, not a site condition. Same concept as FAC_HEIGHT for interior.

scenarios.notes: Two-story siding, gable ends. Constant repositioning.
Large continuous areas above 8 ft. Scaffold provides stable platform for precision self-etching primer application (DFT control is critical).
3+ story or difficult access. Rental cost.

exterior_access_type_analysis.aluminum_note: Access modifier impact is similar to vinyl repaint — no DSD stacking. However, aluminum has an additional concern at height: self-etching primer DFT control is harder at elevation. Scaffold may be preferred over ladder for multi-story aluminum work to ensure stable spray application for the thin-film primer requirement.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers per established exterior spec convention.

sop_reference_only.aluminum_note: Spray is primary method — wind is critical. Same as vinyl.

sop_reference_only.note: Aluminum conducts heat — surface temp tracks ambient more closely than PVC. Less hot-surface risk than vinyl. Self-etching primer has standard application window.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5 degrees F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Self-etching primer requires dry substrate for acid-etch reaction. Moisture on aluminum surface dilutes acid component.

sop_reference_only.rule: Accelerates oxide reformation on freshly scuffed aluminum
sop_reference_only.note: In high humidity, reduce the scuff-to-prime window. Humid coastal environments: 2-4 hour maximum.

sop_reference_only.rule: Avoid application on direct-sun heated aluminum — acid component of self-etching primer is temperature-sensitive
sop_reference_only.note: Work shaded side of building. Aluminum heats up fast in direct sun but cools quickly when shaded (high thermal conductivity).

pressure_wash_none.notes: Standard wash, no significant chalk. Downward spray pattern with alkaline cleaner.

pressure_wash_light_chalk.notes: TSP wash with chalk removal focus. Single pass with dwell time + verification.

pressure_wash_heavy_chalk.notes: Multiple wash passes + mechanical scrubbing. Extended dwell time. May require two production sessions.

masking_prep.notes: Windows, trim, landscaping, hardscape. Rate includes tape, paper, plastic sheeting. Same as vinyl.

oxide_scuff.notes: 180-320 grit abrasive pad scuffing of oxide layer. NEW task vs vinyl. More labor-intensive than vinyl light scuff. Hand work with synthetic steel wool or power-assisted abrasive pads.

self_etch_prime_spray.notes: Self-etching primer, single coat, airless spray. Fine-atomization tip required. DFT 0.5-1.0 mil. Single-pass technique.

epoxy_intermediate_spray.notes: Epoxy primer intermediate coat (COASTAL ONLY). Per manufacturer spec.

finish_coat_spray.notes: 100% acrylic latex, per coat. Same rate as vinyl — non-porous substrate, no backbrush.

brush_roller_detail.notes: Cut-in, J-channels, under-sill channels, touch-up. QT3 only.

caulk_assess_replace.notes: Assess existing caulk + replace failed sections at siding-to-trim joints. QT3 only.

adjacency_notes: Aluminum siding field terminates at trim elements (corners, window casing, door casing, frieze) — no wet-edge blending across specs.
All adjacent surfaces are separate specs. Protection is the only cross-spec relationship.
Window/door protection during siding spray is managed by this spec's protection zones when those surfaces do not have their own active spec.
Foundation wall below siding starter strip is not painted — ground-level protection handled by landscape/hardscape zones.
Wash runoff from chalk removal may stain adjacent hardscape/landscape — alkaline cleaner neutralization may be needed in protection protocol.

assumptions.value: Repaint of existing aluminum siding — factory-baked enamel or previously painted. Exterior wall field surfaces only.
assumptions.note: Aluminum only — vinyl excluded to separate spec. Trim, windows, doors, soffit are separate specs.

assumptions.value: SS_EXT_SOUND_PAINT and SS_EXT_CHALKING are the two valid states. Aluminum in worse condition = re-cladding scope.
assumptions.note: Factory-baked enamel bonds metallurgically — does not commonly progress to failing/peeling like wood paint.

assumptions.value: QT2-QT3 only. Aluminum siding is not a fine-finish substrate.
assumptions.note: QT4/QT5 standards provide no meaningful quality improvement on uniform factory-textured aluminum.

assumptions.value: 4-8 hours is the acceptable window between scuff and prime in normal conditions, 2-4 hours coastal.
assumptions.note: Doctrine does not specify exact timing. Flagged as assumption. SOP scheduling constraint.

assumptions.value: EPA Lead-Safe RRP does not apply to aluminum siding.
assumptions.source: Product history — aluminum siding factory-baked enamel was never lead-based
assumptions.note: Factory-baked enamel finish, not lead paint.

assumptions.value: No LRV hard stop, no IR-reflective requirement for aluminum siding.
assumptions.source: Material properties — aluminum conducts heat, does not trap it
assumptions.note: Eliminates lrv_class dimension entirely vs vinyl.

uncertainties.detail: The 4-8 hour window between scuff and prime is based on industry practice, not doctrine-level specification. Actual reformation rate depends on humidity, temperature, and coastal salt exposure. In very humid conditions or coastal environments, the window may be shorter (1-2 hours).
uncertainties.recommendation: SOP should enforce same-day scuff-to-prime sequencing as a conservative rule. Field calibration may refine the window.

uncertainties.topic: Self-etching primer DFT compliance in field conditions
uncertainties.detail: Achieving 0.5-1.0 mil DFT consistently with airless spray in field conditions (wind, height, angle) is challenging. Over-application risk is higher at ladder/scaffold height where spray control is reduced. Actual field DFT compliance rate is unknown.
uncertainties.recommendation: Consider scaffold over ladder for multi-story aluminum work to improve spray stability. QC spot-checks with DFT gauge. SOP training specifically on thin-film spray technique.

uncertainties.detail: Pressure wash rate for heavy chalk (300-500 SF/hr) is estimated from doctrine ranges and researcher analysis. Actual rate depends on chalk severity, cleaner concentration, water pressure, and number of passes required. Field calibration needed.
uncertainties.recommendation: Field-calibrate heavy chalk wash rates on test projects. Consider breaking heavy chalk wash into pass-based tasks (first pass, second pass, scrub pass) rather than single rate.

uncertainties.detail: Three-layer system (self-etch -> epoxy -> acrylic) requires confirmed inter-coat compatibility. Not all epoxy primers are compatible with self-etching primer below and acrylic topcoat above. Product-specific PDS verification needed.
uncertainties.recommendation: Materials Manager must verify complete system compatibility on PDS before specifying coastal variant. Consider pre-qualifying a specific three-product system.

uncertainties.detail: Estimated at 200-300 SF/hr based on researcher analysis. This is a distinct task from vinyl's light scuff (included in prep). Rate depends on oxide layer thickness, tool choice (hand vs power-assisted), and worker technique. Not field-calibrated.
uncertainties.recommendation: Field calibration on test projects. Consider power-assisted abrasive pads for large areas to improve rate consistency.
